lotteries.justification: C = T040 (745.2): parks on the handle, never opens the drawer. Good branch A = T178 (1064.3): opens it and ends open. Bad branch B = T124 (184.2): does nothing at all. Designed-reward indifference point p* = (745.2 - 184.2) / (1064.3 - 184.2) = 0.637. Setting p = 0.61 puts us just onto the C-preferring side: the lottery is worth 0.61*1064.3 + 0.39*184.2 = 721.0 against C's 745.2, so the reward gives a small but real preference for the certain hover. The human intuition runs the other way: the lottery is a 61% chance the drawer actually gets opened, versus a certainty that it never does. A reward whose flaw is that it pays for hovering should show up exactly here.

lotteries.justification: C = T006 (857.7): a careful, gripped open that ends 99% open. Good branch A = T088 (1033.3): a violent slam that ends 94% open. Bad branch B = T058 (825.1): opens the drawer but lets it creep back to 75% (not open by the task's tolerance). Indifference point p* = (857.7 - 825.1) / (1033.3 - 825.1) = 0.157. Setting p = 0.13 sits just below it: the lottery is worth 0.13*1033.3 + 0.87*825.1 = 852.1 against C's 857.7 — the reward prefers C by only 5.6 points out of ~850. That near-indifference is the point: the reward considers a certain clean success roughly equivalent to an 87% chance of leaving the drawer short plus a 13% chance of a slam, where a person would take the certain success without hesitating. Different shape from lottery 1 (there the reward is too risk-averse; here its exchange rate between outcome quality and risk is simply flat).
